name: Second Polish Republic
info: The Polish state reborn at the end of the First World War after more than a century of partitions, which won the Polish–Soviet War, fell under Piłsudski's Sanacja regime and was destroyed by the German and Soviet invasions of 1939.

facts.founder: Józef Piłsudski, Chief of State from 14 November 1918, after the Regency Council announced the restoration of independence on 7 October 1918
facts.predecessor: Kingdom of Poland (1917–1918) under the Regency Council; before it, the Austrian, Prussian and Russian partitions
facts.successor: German and Soviet occupation (the General Government, lands incorporated into Nazi Germany and annexed to the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic and the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic); the Polish government-in-exile and the Polish Underground State

t: Poland re-emerged as a sovereign state in 1918, and its borders were fixed only after a series of wars from 1918 to 1921, above all the Polish–Soviet War, which ended in a decisive Polish victory.

A parliamentary democracy under the Small Constitution of 1919 gave way to the Sanacja regime after Józef Piłsudski's coup of May 1926; elections from 1930 were manipulated and opposition activists were sent to Bereza Kartuska prison.
Almost a third of its people belonged to minorities, and after Piłsudski's death in 1935 the government openly discriminated against Jewish and, to a lesser extent, Ukrainian and Belarusian citizens.
dyk: Neighbouring cities of the new republic had belonged to different empires, so there was no direct railway connection between Warsaw and Kraków until 1934, and the country began with five different currencies.
ev: The Regency Council announces the restoration of Polish independence on 7 October, and on 14 November transfers its authority to Józef Piłsudski as Chief of State
The Treaty of Versailles confirms the rebirth of Poland, and the Small Constitution of 1919 establishes a parliamentary democracy
The Polish–Soviet War, fought since 1919, ends in a decisive Polish victory
The eastern borders are settled diplomatically and recognised by the League of Nations
Prime Minister Władysław Grabski introduces the złoty, which brings the hyperinflation under control without foreign loans or aid
Piłsudski takes power in a military coup in May and establishes the Sanacja regime
An authoritarian constitution is approved in the spring, and Piłsudski dies shortly after
Germany and Slovakia invade on 1 September and the Soviet Union on 17 September, and organised resistance ends on 6 October after the Battle of Kock

sections.foundation:
After more than a century of partitions between Austria, Prussia and Russia, Poland re-emerged as a sovereign state in 1917–1918. Germany had set up the puppet Kingdom of Poland on 14 January 1917, governed from October 1917 by a Regency Council, which on 7 October 1918 announced its intention to restore Polish independence. In November socialists set up a Provisional People's Government under Ignacy Daszyński in Lublin. Józef Piłsudski, freed from a German prison in Magdeburg, returned to Warsaw on 10 November, was made Commander in Chief the next day, and on 14 November received all the Council's authority as Chief of State. Women were granted the vote by his decree of 28 November 1918.

The Treaty of Versailles of June 1919 confirmed the rebirth of Poland, but its borders were won in a series of wars fought by the new Polish Army from 1918 to 1921: the Polish–Ukrainian War from Lwów, the Greater Poland uprising, the Polish–Czechoslovak War over Trans-Olza, the Polish–Lithuanian War, three Silesian Uprisings and, most critical, the Polish–Soviet War (1919–1921), which ended in a decisive Polish victory. The eastern frontier was settled in 1922 and recognised by the League of Nations.
sections.socioeconomy:
The republic inherited three economic systems, five currencies and few railway links, as well as the destruction of the First World War and the Polish–Soviet War. The west, "Poland A", was far more developed than "Poland B" in the east, and industry lay mostly in Upper Silesia and Zagłębie Dąbrowskie, with textiles at Łódź and oil at Borysław and Drohobycz. In 1924 Władysław Grabski introduced the złoty, which mastered the hyperinflation. In 1921, 75% of the people lived in the countryside, and in 1929 agriculture made up 65% of GNP; rural overpopulation brought chronic unemployment and, among the Hutsul counties, permanent starvation. After the Great Depression Eugeniusz Kwiatkowski's plans built the port of Gdynia, the Polish Coal Trunk-Line from Upper Silesia, and the Central Industrial Region, with the new steel town of Stalowa Wola.

The 1921 census counted 25.7 million inhabitants, and by 1939 an estimated 35.1 million. In 1931, 69% were Polish, 14% Ukrainian, around 10% Jewish and 3% Belarusian; Poland had the second largest Jewish population in the world. Compulsory schooling from 1919 cut illiteracy from a third in 1921 to 18% in 1937, and by 1939 around 50,000 students were in higher education, 28% of university students being women.
sections.military:
The constitution of 1921 required all male citizens to serve on reaching 21. Interwar Poland kept 270,000 soldiers on active duty in 37 infantry divisions, 11 cavalry brigades and two armoured brigades, with another 700,000 in the reserves. Training was thorough, but equipment lagged behind Nazi Germany's, rearmament was slowed by confidence in Western support and by budget difficulties, and the command system was obsolete. The air force shrank during modernisation in the mid-1930s, to 417 planes in 1936, and the navy, based at Gdynia, had 18 ships in 1939.

In September 1939 the army put almost one million soldiers in the field, with 4,300 guns, around 1,000 armoured vehicles, most of them outclassed tankettes, and 745 aircraft. Against the Germans it lost about 70,000 killed and missing and some 420,000 prisoners, and against the Red Army 6,000 to 7,000 casualties and 250,000 prisoners; it killed or left missing 20,000 German soldiers and destroyed or badly damaged 674 tanks. The story that Polish cavalry charged German tanks with lances is a myth, born of misreporting of a sabre charge by the 18th Lancers near Krojanty on 1 September, which wiped out a German infantry formation.
sections.governance:
From 1919 to 1926 the republic was a parliamentary democracy under the Small Constitution of 1919, with a president elected by parliament and of limited powers. The main parties were the Polish Socialist Party, the National Democrats, peasant parties, Christian Democrats and the parties of the minorities, among them the Bund and the Ukrainian National Democratic Alliance. Frequent changes of government and charges of corruption made politicians unpopular; besides Piłsudski, the leading figures were the peasant activist Wincenty Witos, three times prime minister, and the right-wing leader Roman Dmowski.

After his coup of May 1926 Piłsudski promised to heal politics of excessive partisanship, and his regime was called Sanacja. The 1928 elections were still considered free, but those of 1930, 1935 and 1938 were manipulated, with opposition activists sent to Bereza Kartuska prison, and the Camp of National Unity won huge majorities. An authoritarian constitution was approved in the spring of 1935, just before Piłsudski died; the country was then led by President Ignacy Mościcki, Foreign Minister Józef Beck and Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły. The state was divided into gminy, powiaty and voivodeships, a system that passed into the Third Polish Republic.
sections.impact:
Interwar Poland was the sixth largest country in Europe in 1938, and Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań, Wilno and Lwów became major European cities with internationally acclaimed universities. Polish science was known for the Lwów School of Mathematics, the Kraków School of Mathematics and the Warsaw School of Mathematics and the Lwów–Warsaw school of logic and philosophy; Rudolf Weigl invented a vaccine against typhus, and Bronisław Malinowski was among the most important anthropologists of the century. Literature was led in the 1920s by the poets of the Skamanderites, and the country had 103 theatres and about one million radios.

Its treatment of minorities left deep scars. From the 1920s Jews were excluded from government bank loans and public employment, and from the 1930s limits were placed on their admission to universities and to the medical and legal professions; the Camp of National Unity drafted anti-Semitic legislation and advocated mass emigration of Jews, and William W. Hagen writes that by 1939 Polish Jews were threatened with conditions similar to those in Nazi Germany. Ukrainians were refused territorial autonomy, their language was restricted, and Ukrainians in Eastern Galicia were subjected to the Pacification of 1930.
sections.decline:
Relations with its neighbours were hostile for much of the period: a customs war with the Weimar Republic lasted from June 1925 until 1933, and in 1938 Poland issued an ultimatum to Lithuania and annexed Trans-Olza from Czechoslovakia. One week after Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, Germany and Slovakia attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, and the Soviets attacked eastern Poland on 17 September. Warsaw fell on 28 September after a twenty-day siege, and open organised resistance ended on 6 October 1939 after the Battle of Kock. The lack of promised aid from the Western Allies contributed to the defeat.

Poland never surrendered. It fought on through the Polish government-in-exile, established in Paris and then London, and the Polish Underground State. Germany incorporated part of the occupied land and made the rest the General Government; the Soviet Union annexed the east to the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic and the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, and Lithuania took the Wilno area. The government-in-exile claimed to be the only legal representative of the nation until 1990, when the last president in exile, Ryszard Kaczorowski, handed the presidential insignia to Lech Wałęsa.

summary: The Second Polish Republic was the Polish state of 1918 to 1939, reborn after the partitions and enlarged by victory in the Polish–Soviet War. A parliamentary democracy turned authoritarian under Piłsudski's Sanacja, it built universities, Gdynia and new industry while discriminating against its large minorities, and was destroyed by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939.

Norman Davies, God's Playground: A History of Poland, vol. 2: 1795 to the Present (Oxford University Press, 1981)
R. F. Leslie et al., The History of Poland since 1863 (Cambridge University Press, 1980)

Z. Landau and J. Tomaszewski, The Polish Economy in the Twentieth Century (Routledge, 1985)

pointDescs.1918: The Regency Council announces independence on 7 October, and Piłsudski becomes Chief of State on 14 November as border wars begin.
pointDescs.1919: The Treaty of Versailles confirms Poland's rebirth, the Small Constitution is adopted, and compulsory schooling is introduced.
pointDescs.1921: The Polish–Soviet War ends in a decisive Polish victory, and the census counts 25.7 million inhabitants.
pointDescs.1922: The eastern borders are settled and recognised by the League of Nations, and Wilno University opens as the sixth university.
pointDescs.1924: The złoty replaces the marka and brings the hyperinflation under control.
pointDescs.1925: The Weimar Republic begins a customs war against Poland that lasts nearly a decade.
pointDescs.1926: Piłsudski takes power in the May coup and establishes the Sanacja regime.
pointDescs.1929: Growth of GDP per capita averages 5.24% a year through the 1920s, by a 2010 estimate, and LOT Polish Airlines is established.
pointDescs.1930: The Great Depression strikes, elections are manipulated, and Ukrainians in Eastern Galicia are subjected to the Pacification.
pointDescs.1935: An authoritarian constitution is approved and Piłsudski dies; the government begins openly to discriminate against Jews.
pointDescs.1936: Kwiatkowski's plans begin the Central Industrial Region as the economy recovers from the Depression.
pointDescs.1938: Poland is the sixth largest country in Europe and annexes Trans-Olza from Czechoslovakia.
pointDescs.1939: Germany, Slovakia and the Soviet Union invade, and organised resistance ends on 6 October after the Battle of Kock.

notes: The article gives Warsaw no 'capital' label; Warsaw is where Piłsudski took power and the seat of government throughout.
Growth figures conflict (2010 estimate 0.34% a year in 1929-1938 against a study dated 2026 of 2.5% a year in 1924-1938); only the 1920s figure is used, attributed.
The 1936 point dates the Central Industrial Region from 'the mid-1930s'; the article gives no exact year for its start.
The article does not date the Peace of Riga; the 1921 event uses the war's end date given (1919–1921).
